title: Print Linked List
description: Walk the list and print each value followed by a space; end with a newline.
story: Everything in linked lists starts here: `for (Node c = head; c != null; c = c.next)`.
howToThink: "Visit every node once" is just traversal — one pointer, no extra structure.
Walk with `c = head` and step `c = c.next` until `c` is null.
This loop is the atom of every LL problem; know it cold.
pitfalls: Loop while `c != null`, not `c.next != null`, or you drop the last node.
Empty list (`head == null`) should print nothing, not crash.
Advance `c = c.next` inside the loop or you spin forever.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
c = head
while c != null: print c.val + ' '; c = c.next
print newline
solutions.story: If you can't write this from muscle memory, every other LL problem will hurt.
solutions.plain: Use a pointer c starting at head. While c is not null, print c.val followed by a space, then advance c = c.next. Print a final newline.
solutions.tale: The elder grips the first door handle in her left hand. She speaks its number aloud, lets go, grabs the next door handle. She repeats until her hand finds empty air — then she announces the end with a bow.
approach: Initialise a pointer c at head.
While c is not null, print c.val with a trailing space.
Advance c = c.next.
After the loop, print a newline.

plain: Walk the singly linked list from the head, printing each node's value followed by a space. End with a newline. This is the most basic linked-list traversal — every other LL problem builds on this loop.
tale: A village elder walks down a long path of houses, each holding a number on a sign. At every house she calls out the number to the crowd behind her, then walks to the next house. When she reaches the end of the path (there is no next house), she returns to the square and bows.

title: Reverse Linked List
description: Reverse a singly linked list in-place in one pass.
story: Three pointers, one mantra: save next, flip the arrow, slide forward. prev becomes the new head.
plain: Walk the list once. At every node, flip its `next` arrow to point BACKWARDS instead of forwards. You need three pointers to do this safely: prev (where you came from), curr (where you are), next (where you were about to go — saved before you smash the arrow). When you fall off the end, prev is the new head.
tale: Imagine a long line of children holding hands, each child's right hand clasping the next child's left. You are told to reverse the line without anyone letting go for more than a heartbeat. So you go to the first child and say: 'remember the hand you were holding (that is `next`). Now let go of it. Now take the hand of the empty space behind you (that is `prev`).' Then you walk to the child who was on the right, and you whisper the same instructions. Heartbeat by heartbeat, the line turns around. When you reach the end, the last child you spoke to is now leading the parade.
howToThink: "Reverse in place" means re-point each `next` backward as you walk.
That needs three pointers: `prev`, `curr`, and a saved `next`.
Save `next` before flipping, else you lose the rest of the list.
When `curr` falls off the end, `prev` is the new head.
pitfalls: Cache `next = curr.next` before `curr.next = prev` or the tail is gone.
Return `prev`, not `head` — `head` is now the tail.
Start `prev = null` so the old head correctly ends pointing at null.

solutions.label: Iterative (optimal)
solutions.plain: Keep three references: prev (starts null), curr (starts at head), and next (a temp). On each iteration, save curr.next into next, point curr.next at prev, then slide prev = curr and curr = next. When curr becomes null, prev is the new head.
solutions.tale: Three friends — Past, Present, Future — walk down the line together. Present grabs the hand of the next child (Future) before letting go, then turns and gives that hand back to Past. Then everyone shuffles one seat forward: Past becomes who Present was, Present becomes who Future was, and a new Future appears. When Future steps off the cliff at the end, Past is left standing as the head of the reversed line.
approach: Initialise prev = null and curr = head.
While curr is not null, snapshot next = curr.next so you don't lose the tail.
Flip the arrow: curr.next = prev.
Slide prev forward: prev = curr.
Slide curr forward: curr = next.
When the loop exits, curr is null and prev points to the original last node — return prev as the new head.
solutions.pseudocode:
prev = null, curr = head
while curr:
  next = curr.next
  curr.next = prev
  prev = curr; curr = next
return prev
solutions.story: The dance: NEXT save, NEXT flip, PREV step, CURR step. Repeat until curr falls off the end.

solutions.label: Recursive
solutions.plain: Recurse to the end of the list. The deepest call returns the original tail — that is the new head, and it just bubbles up unchanged. On the way back, each call flips one arrow: it makes its successor point back to itself, then severs its own forward arrow.
solutions.tale: A whisper travels down the line: 'pass it on, the last person should turn around.' The whisper reaches the last child who turns. As the whisper bounces back, each child it passes turns around in turn, until the whole line has flipped. Beautiful, but every child waited on the stack for the whisper to come back — if the line is a million children long, the stack will collapse.
approach: Base case: if head is null or head.next is null, return head — nothing to flip.
Recurse on head.next; capture the returned new head of the reversed sub-list.
Flip the link between head and its old successor: head.next.next = head.
Sever head's old forward pointer: head.next = null (this becomes the new tail).
Return the captured new head all the way back up the call stack.
solutions.pseudocode:
if !head or !head.next: return head
newHead = reverse(head.next)
head.next.next = head
head.next = null
return newHead
solutions.story: Recurse to the tail, then flip on the way back. Elegant but blows the stack on long lists.

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
description: Each node has next AND a random pointer to any node (or null). Return a deep copy.
story: HashMap version: pass 1 clones, pass 2 wires next + random using the map. Interweaving version: insert clones between originals → set randoms in place → unzip the two lists.
howToThink: A `random` pointer means you must map each old node to its clone.
HashMap old→new is the clearest fix; O(1) space needs the interweaving trick.
Interweaving: splice each clone right after its original, so `orig.next` IS the clone.
Then `clone.random = orig.random.next`, and unzip the two lists at the end.
pitfalls: Do it in three separate passes — interleave, wire randoms, then unzip.
Null-check `c.random` before reading `c.random.next`.
Restore the originals' `next` while unzipping, don't leave them interleaved.
Return `null` up front if `head` is null.

solutions.label: HashMap (clearest)
solutions.pseudocode:
pass 1: map[orig] = new Node(orig.val)
pass 2: for each orig:
  map[orig].next   = map[orig.next]
  map[orig].random = map[orig.random]
solutions.story: Hash old → new. Then re-wire from old's pointers but look up new's nodes through the map.
solutions.plain: Pass 1: walk the original list and for every node create a fresh clone (same value, no pointers wired yet); store old->new in a HashMap. Pass 2: walk the original again; for each old node, set clone.next = map.get(old.next) and clone.random = map.get(old.random). HashMap.get(null) returns null, which auto-handles the random-null and tail-null cases. Return map.get(head).
solutions.tale: The archivist first writes a blank duplicate of every line and notes 'old 1 -> new 1, old 2 -> new 2' in her ledger. Then she walks the old scroll again: at each line she follows the original's next and random arrows, looks up the corresponding new line in her ledger, and draws the equivalent arrow on the duplicate. By the end every arrow on the new scroll points to a new line.
approach: Pass 1: create a HashMap<RandomListNode, RandomListNode>. For every node c in the original, put map(c -> new RandomListNode(c.label)).
Pass 2: for every node c, set map.get(c).next = map.get(c.next) and map.get(c).random = map.get(c.random).
Return map.get(head).
Edge case: map.get(null) returns null, which correctly handles tail's next and any node's null random.

solutions.label: Interweaving (O(1) space)
solutions.pseudocode:
Pass 1: insert clone after each original (A→A'→B→B'…).
Pass 2: clone.random = original.random.next.
Pass 3: unzip the two lists, restoring originals.
solutions.story: Smuggle the clones inside the original list to skip the hash map. Three passes, no extra storage.
solutions.plain: Three passes, no HashMap. Pass 1: insert a clone immediately AFTER each original (1 -> 1' -> 2 -> 2' -> ...). Pass 2: for every original c, set c.next.random = c.random.next — the clone of c's random is sitting right after c.random. Pass 3: separate the two interleaved lists by re-routing pointers.
solutions.tale: The clever archivist places each new blank line immediately after the corresponding old line. Now setting random arrows is easy: 'new line for old 3, your random is the new line directly after old 3's random'. After that, she splits the interleaved scroll into two: every other line goes to the new scroll, the original lines stay where they were.
approach: Return null if head is null.
Pass 1: walk c = head, stepping c = c.next.next; create a clone of c, set clone.next = c.next, then c.next = clone.
Pass 2: walk c = head, stepping c = c.next.next; if c.random is not null, set c.next.random = c.random.next.
Pass 3: build the new list. Use dummy + t pointer. For each c, set t.next = c.next, t = t.next, c.next = c.next.next.
Return dummy.next.

plain: Each node has the usual next pointer plus a random pointer that may point to any node in the list (or null). You need a deep copy — clone every node with the same next and random topology, but pointing only at the new nodes. Two well-known approaches: (1) a HashMap from old to new in two passes, or (2) interweave clones inside the original list to avoid extra space.
tale: An archivist must copy an ancient scroll where each line not only follows the next line but also points to one other random line elsewhere. She must produce a perfect duplicate where every random arrow lands on the new scroll's line, not the old one. There are two ways: (1) she keeps a paired ledger — 'old line 7 means new line 7' — and consults it twice, or (2) she cleverly interleaves the new lines between the old ones, making the random arrows easy to copy without any external bookkeeping.

title: Insert at Position
description: Insert a new node with value B at 0-indexed position C. C ≥ length → insert at tail.
story: Walk to node at index C-1, then splice. Use a dummy node so 'insert at head' isn't a special case.
howToThink: Inserting anywhere, including the head, screams "use a dummy node."
A dummy before head means position 0 needs no special branch.
Walk `prev` to the node just before the slot, then splice.
Wire the new node's `next` first, then re-point `prev.next` to it.
pitfalls: Set `node.next = prev.next` before `prev.next = node`, or you lose the tail.
Stop the walk early when `prev.next == null` so `C >= length` lands at the tail.
Return `dummy.next`, not `head` — the head may have changed.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
dummy.next = head; prev = dummy
for i in 0..C-1: if prev.next == null break; prev = prev.next
newNode.next = prev.next; prev.next = newNode
return dummy.next
solutions.story: Dummy node = no edge case for the head. Walk to the predecessor and splice.
solutions.plain: Create a dummy node whose next is head — this removes the special case for inserting at position 0. Walk prev forward exactly C steps OR until prev.next is null. Build the new node, set node.next = prev.next, then prev.next = node. Return dummy.next.
solutions.tale: The scribe pins a blank dummy card at the front of the list. He walks his finger forward C times (or stops early if the list ends). At the stopping point, he creates the new card, copies the predecessor's forward arrow onto it, then re-points the predecessor's arrow to the new card.
approach: Create dummy = new ListNode(0) with dummy.next = head.
Initialise prev = dummy.
Loop i from 0 to pos-1 while prev.next is not null: advance prev = prev.next.
Create the new node with value.
Stitch: node.next = prev.next, prev.next = node.
Return dummy.next.

title: Delete at Position
description: Delete the B-th node (0-indexed). If B is out of range, return list unchanged.
story: Walk to predecessor, skip the doomed node. Dummy node makes 'delete head' just like any other.
howToThink: Deleting any node, head included, is the dummy-node pattern again.
Walk `prev` to the node before the victim, then skip over it.
`prev.next = prev.next.next` unlinks the doomed node.
pitfalls: Bail out if the walk hits `prev.next == null` — index is out of range.
Guard `prev.next != null` before dereferencing `prev.next.next`.
Return `dummy.next` so deleting the head still returns the right list.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
dummy.next = head; prev = dummy
for i in 0..B-1: if prev.next == null return head; prev = prev.next
if prev.next != null: prev.next = prev.next.next
return dummy.next
solutions.story: Find the node just before the victim, then point past it.
solutions.plain: Create dummy with dummy.next = head. Walk prev forward B steps; if prev.next becomes null mid-walk, position is out of range — return head. Otherwise, if prev.next is not null, set prev.next = prev.next.next to bypass the victim. Return dummy.next.
solutions.tale: The archivist pins a dummy entry at the top. He walks his finger forward B times, checking at every step that the next entry still exists. If he runs out before reaching B, the requested deletion is impossible and he walks away. Otherwise he erases the predecessor's arrow and redraws it past the victim.
approach: Create dummy with dummy.next = head and prev = dummy.
Loop i from 0 to pos-1: if prev.next is null, return head (out of range).
Otherwise advance prev = prev.next.
After the loop, if prev.next is not null, set prev.next = prev.next.next.
Return dummy.next.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
description: Sorted list → each value appears once. Skip consecutive duplicates.
story: Walk with one pointer. If next equals current, jump over next.
howToThink: "Sorted" means duplicates sit next to each other — compare `c.val` with `c.next.val`.
One pointer suffices; splice out the neighbor when they match.
Key catch: don't advance after deleting — the next one might also be a dup.
pitfalls: Only advance `c` in the `else` branch, never after a splice.
Loop while `c != null && c.next != null` so `c.next.val` is safe.
Return the original `head` — it never changes here (no dummy needed).

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
c = head
while c && c.next:
  if c.val == c.next.val: c.next = c.next.next
  else c = c.next
return head
solutions.story: Don't advance when you delete — there might be another duplicate right behind it.
solutions.plain: Use a single pointer c = head. While c is not null and c.next is not null: if c.val equals c.next.val, set c.next = c.next.next (don't advance c). Otherwise advance c = c.next. Return head.
solutions.tale: The clerk's finger sits on the first name. He compares it with the next. Same? Erase the next, finger stays. Different? Finger moves forward. He stops at the last name.
approach: Initialise c = head.
While c and c.next are both non-null:
If c.val equals c.next.val, bypass: c.next = c.next.next (don't advance c).
Else advance c = c.next.
Return head.

title: Remove Nth Node from End
description: Remove the B-th node counted from the end in one pass. If B ≥ length, remove the head.
story: Stretch a rubber band of length B between two pointers. Slide both until fast falls off — slow lands on the predecessor.
howToThink: "Nth from the end in one pass" is the fixed-gap two-pointer trick.
Move `fast` B steps ahead, then slide both until `fast` hits the end.
`slow` then lands on the node just before the victim.
A dummy makes removing the head no different from any other node.
pitfalls: If `fast.next` goes null while advancing B steps, B >= length — remove the head.
Start both pointers at `dummy`, not `head`, to keep the gap correct.
Return `dummy.next`, since the head itself may be the one removed.

solutions.label: Optimal — two pointers
solutions.pseudocode:
dummy.next = head; fast = slow = dummy
advance fast B steps
while fast.next: fast = fast.next; slow = slow.next
slow.next = slow.next.next
return dummy.next
solutions.story: Dummy makes the 'remove first' case stop being special. Two pointers, gap of B, slide together.
solutions.plain: Create dummy with dummy.next = head; fast = slow = dummy. Move fast forward B times — if fast.next becomes null along the way, B is at or beyond list length, so remove the head. Then slide fast and slow together until fast.next is null. slow now points at the predecessor; set slow.next = slow.next.next.
solutions.tale: The dummy is the surveyor's starting cairn. The scout sprints B paces forward. If the scout falls off the road already, the only milestone to remove is the very first one. Otherwise, both walk together — when the scout reaches the very last milestone, the surveyor stands at the milestone just before the doomed one, and removes it.
approach: Create dummy with dummy.next = head; fast = slow = dummy.
Loop i from 0 to B-1: if fast.next is null, return head == null ? null : head.next (B exceeds length, remove head).
Otherwise advance fast = fast.next.
While fast.next is not null, advance both: fast = fast.next, slow = slow.next.
Bypass: slow.next = slow.next.next.
Return dummy.next.

title: Reverse Linked List II (Partial)
description: Reverse positions B through C (1-indexed), in-place, one pass.
story: Walk to the node before B. Reverse exactly (C − B + 1) nodes by repeatedly lifting the next node to the front of the segment. Stitch back.
howToThink: "Reverse positions B..C" is a segment reversal — anchor the node before B.
A dummy lets `pre` sit before the head even when B == 1.
Front-insertion: repeatedly lift `then` and re-insert it right after `pre`.
Exactly `C - B` lifts flips the segment and stitches both ends automatically.
pitfalls: Walk `pre` only `B - 1` steps (loop from 1), not B.
`start` stays fixed as the segment's eventual tail — don't move it.
Handle `B == C` (and null head) as a no-op up front.
Do the four re-link steps in order so no pointer is lost.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.pseudocode:
dummy.next = head; pre = dummy
advance pre B-1 steps
start = pre.next; then = start.next
for k in 1..(C-B):
  start.next = then.next
  then.next  = pre.next
  pre.next   = then
  then = start.next
return dummy.next
solutions.story: Front-insertion: keep lifting `then` to the front of the segment. After (C-B) lifts the segment is reversed and stitched.
solutions.plain: Use a dummy node so pre can start before head. Walk pre to position B-1. Let start = pre.next (the first node of the segment, will become the new tail) and then = start.next. Front-insert (C-B) times: detach 'then', re-insert immediately after pre. After the loop, return dummy.next.
solutions.tale: She pins a dummy clip at the front. Walks her thumb B-1 steps. Identifies 'start' (the first segment page) and 'then' (the one right after). She repeatedly: unhooks 'then' from start, hooks it to whatever pre points at, hooks pre directly to 'then'. After C-B lifts, the segment is reversed in place.
approach: If head is null or B == C, no change needed; return head.
Create dummy with dummy.next = head; pre = dummy.
Walk pre forward B-1 times (loop i from 1 to B-1).
Set start = pre.next (the eventual segment tail) and then = start.next.
Loop k from 0 to C-B-1: start.next = then.next; then.next = pre.next; pre.next = then; then = start.next.
Return dummy.next.

plain: Reverse the segment from position B to position C (1-indexed), in place, in one pass. Walk a 'pre' pointer to the node just before position B. Then, exactly C-B times, perform a 'front-insertion': lift the node after 'start' and re-insert it right after 'pre'. After the loop, the segment is reversed and stitched correctly to both sides.
tale: A bookbinder must flip pages B through C of a long bound book without removing the cover. She places her thumb on the binding right before page B. Then she lifts page (B+1) out and slips it in right after her thumb. Then she lifts the new next page and slips IT in right after her thumb. Repeat C-B times. The segment ends up reversed, and the binding holding the book together is intact.

title: Reverse Linked List in K Groups
description: Reverse the list B at a time. B always divides the length.
story: Reverse the first K. Recursively reverse the rest. Connect the old head (now tail) to the recursive result.
howToThink: "Reverse every K nodes" is block reversal — reverse K, then stitch to the rest.
First check a full group of K exists before touching pointers.
Iterative version keeps `prevGroupEnd` to re-link each flipped block.
Reverse until `curr == nextGroup`, so each block's tail points into the next group.
pitfalls: Confirm K nodes remain first; leave a short trailing group untouched.
After reversing, `prevGroupEnd.next = kth` then advance `prevGroupEnd = groupStart` (the new tail).
Seed `prev = nextGroup` so the block's tail links forward correctly.
Return `dummy.next`, since the first group's reversal moves the head.

solutions.label: Recursive
solutions.pseudocode:
if length < K: return head
reverse first K nodes (standard reversal)
old head.next = reverseK(nextGroupHead, K)
return newHead of this group
solutions.story: Reverse K, then say 'do the same to what's left, please.' The recursion handles the rest.
solutions.plain: First count K nodes from head. If fewer than K remain, return head unchanged (problem says B divides length, but this is the safe edge). Otherwise reverse the first K nodes via the standard 3-pointer reverse. The original head is now the tail of the reversed block; set head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, K) where curr is the (K+1)th node. Return prev (the new head of this block).
solutions.tale: The weaver counts K beads. She flips them in place. Now the old head is at the tail of the flipped block. She instructs her apprentice: 'Take the remainder and do the same.' The apprentice returns the new head of the remainder, which the weaver attaches to her flipped block's tail.
approach: Count K nodes starting from head. If fewer than K remain (cnt < K), return head unchanged.
Standard 3-pointer reverse: prev = null, curr = head; loop K times — nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nxt.
After the loop, the original head is the tail of the reversed block. Set head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, K).
Return prev (new head of this reversed block).

solutions.label: Iterative
solutions.pseudocode:
dummy; prevGroupEnd = dummy
Loop:
  reach K-th node (if can't, break)
  reverse the K-block
  stitch prevGroupEnd to the new head, set new prevGroupEnd
solutions.story: Same idea, no recursion. Maintain prevGroupEnd to stitch each reversed block back into the chain.
solutions.plain: Use a dummy with dummy.next = head and prevGroupEnd = dummy. Each iteration: walk kth K steps forward from prevGroupEnd — if it falls off, stop. Mark groupStart = prevGroupEnd.next and nextGroup = kth.next. Reverse the K nodes between groupStart and nextGroup using the standard reverse loop, stopping when curr == nextGroup. Then re-stitch: prevGroupEnd.next = kth (new head of reversed block), and advance prevGroupEnd = groupStart (the new tail).
solutions.tale: The weaver pins a dummy anchor at the start. She counts K beads ahead — if she can't, she stops. She flips those K beads, then reattaches the anchor to the new head of the flipped group, and moves the anchor to the new tail. Then she repeats.
approach: Create dummy with dummy.next = head; prevGroupEnd = dummy.
Loop forever: walk kth from prevGroupEnd K steps; if kth becomes null, break.
Capture groupStart = prevGroupEnd.next and nextGroup = kth.next.
Reverse: prev = nextGroup, curr = groupStart; while curr != nextGroup, nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nxt.
Stitch: prevGroupEnd.next = kth (new head of reversed block).
Advance the anchor: prevGroupEnd = groupStart.
Return dummy.next.

plain: Reverse the list in blocks of K nodes. B always divides the length, so no partial block remains. Either: (1) recursively — reverse the first K nodes, then recurse on the rest and connect the old head (now tail) to the recursive result; or (2) iteratively — maintain a 'prevGroupEnd' anchor that stitches each reversed block back into the chain.
tale: A weaver has a long thread of beads in groups of K. She wants every group flipped while leaving the order of the groups themselves intact. She has two methods: (1) flip the first K beads, then tell her apprentice 'do the same to what remains' (recursion handles the rest), or (2) keep a steady anchor between groups — flip the K beads after the anchor, re-attach to the anchor, then move the anchor to the new end of the flipped group and repeat.
